paragraphs: Before publication, she wrote separate notes about what the image showed and what she had learned from conversations. The dish and chair were visible facts; the explanation of their use came from the people she had asked. She checked the opening hours with the owner and identified the photograph's time in the caption. Readers could then understand why that particular moment looked quiet without assuming that every hour was the same.

She also kept a question about shops she had not yet visited. Learning that one bakery was active did not prove that the whole street was doing well. The revised article needed evidence for any wider claim. Her first mistake had been moving too quickly from a small scene to a large conclusion, and she wanted to avoid repeating it in the opposite direction.
rationale: 間接疑問・関係節・動名詞・比較を読み、一瞬の観察と広い一般化の根拠を区別する。

paragraphs: Before starting the trial, Amir met the caretaker to discuss what an inspection would involve. They listed the parts to check and the person who would receive a report if something seemed wrong. A name on a schedule was not enough unless that person understood the task and had agreed to do it. Amir therefore asked the proposed helpers to review the plan. One explained that she would be away for part of the holiday, so the group adjusted the dates. They also decided to record problems during the trial instead of judging it only by the amount of water collected. The smaller version gave them a chance to discover difficulties before expanding the system. Amir's final account included these limits, making the proposal easier to question as well as easier to understand.

paragraphs: For his next training review, the runner wrote down the course and weather beside his times. He knew that a quicker result on an easier route would not prove the same kind of progress. He compared similar sessions when possible and discussed the differences with his coach. The chart was a tool for asking better questions, not a way to guarantee that every future race would be faster.

He also asked the younger runner what she wanted to improve before offering advice. Her main concern was keeping a steady pace during the middle of a race, rather than changing her start. They chose a small goal for the next session and agreed to check it afterward. A useful lesson from his own race could guide their discussion without becoming a rule that everyone had to follow.

paragraphs: For the comparison, the translator asked the assistant to explain what a reader would understand about the child's choice in each version. In one, the custom was named but its connection to the refusal was missing. In the other, a brief explanation made the reason easier to follow without stopping the action for a long lesson. The assistant suggested cutting a sentence that repeated information already clear from the dialogue. They checked that the change preserved the characters' motives and the pace of the scene. Neither version was judged only by its number of familiar words. The notes became a record of why a detail had been kept, explained, or removed. A later reviewer could then question a choice by considering its effect, rather than guessing what the translator had intended.

paragraphs: When planning another dinner, Fumi offered guests a choice about how much to put on their plates. She explained that more food was available, so a small first portion did not mean that anyone had to remain hungry. She paid attention to direct requests instead of trying to read every feeling from the amount left.

Afterward, she asked whether the serving arrangement had been comfortable. One guest said that being able to ask for more made it easier to try an unfamiliar dish. Another preferred to serve herself. Fumi kept these comments as possibilities for future meals, not as a new rule for every guest. Her aim was to make room for different needs while accepting that a friendly evening could not be measured by a single visible sign.
rationale: 間接疑問・関係節・動名詞・受動態を読み、一つの行動から内心を決めつけず選択と確認を重視する姿勢を推論する。
